clue.text: Draw an area of land in hearing

indicators.note: what is in hearing reaches you as a sound, so the ear decides the spelling and not the page

parts.note: a tract is a stretch of open country, and the article runs straight onto it when you say the phrase

explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' wants to be a sketch or a tied match; it is the magnet's sense here, and the rest of the clue is one spoken phrase rather than any spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Draw -> ATTRACT: the magnetic sense of the verb, pulling something towards you rather than sketching it.

clue.text: Dye source in Manila envelope discarded

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the word that follows instead of being clued separately
an envelope is the wrapper round the contents, so throwing it away loses the letter at each end

parts.note: four consecutive letters of the city's name, once the ends have gone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Manila envelope' is a real thing in a stationery cupboard, which is why the setter puts those two words together; only the first of them is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Dye source -> ANIL: the West Indian shrub that indigo is extracted from, so it is the plant behind the colour rather than the colour itself.

clue.text: Extremists in Tory pressure group get ready to print

indicators.note: the extremists of a word are the letters at its two ends, as far from the middle as you can get

parts.note: the two ends of the party's name
the same treatment again, the letters at the front and back of the word
a set is a group of things taken together

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory pressure group' is one phrase in the surface and three separate jobs in the parse: two words plundered for their ends and a third swapped for a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: get ready to print -> TYPESET: to typeset copy is to set it in type, the preparation a page goes through before a press can touch it.

clue.text: The author will read out loud a passage

indicators.note: reading a thing out loud turns it into a sound, and the sound is what the entry has to match

parts.note: the person writing the clue is 'I', and 'I will' shrinks to a single syllable

explanation.walkthrough: Setters call themselves 'the author', 'the setter' or 'this compiler' and mean the one letter I. Everything after that is just the contraction said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: a passage -> AISLE: the walkway between rows of seats or supermarket shelves, a passage you move along rather than one you read.

clue.text: Potentially injurious plants she tilts alarmingly

indicators.note: something done alarmingly is out of control, and letters out of control will not stay in the order given

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, straight from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: 'Potentially injurious' is a long way of saying prickly, and it reads like a warning label on the surface while the two little words beside it quietly hand over every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Potentially injurious plants -> THISTLES: thistles are weeds armoured with spines, so a bare leg brushing one really can come off worse.

clue.text: Fellow gets drink for each girl in 20s

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for fellow, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
a cat drinks by lapping, and to lap up liquid is to drink it
per means for each, as in miles per hour

explanation.walkthrough: The 20s are the 1920s, not an age bracket: bobbed hair, dropped waists and the Charleston are what the definition is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: girl in 20s -> FLAPPER: the fashionable young woman of the 1920s, named for the flapping of her unbuckled galoshes.

clue.text: Spooner's marshland enemy, that shines faintly in mist

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so the pair trade their first letters

parts.note: waterlogged marshy ground is a bog; it hands its B to the word beside it and takes an F in exchange
an enemy is a foe, and with the B swapped in it is the one that rhymes with go — the arc a rainbow makes

explanation.walkthrough: The thing itself is the pale, almost colourless cousin of a rainbow, seen when the sun catches fog: droplets too small to split the light properly.
explanation.definitionFit: that shines faintly in mist -> FOGBOW: a fogbow is a rainbow formed in fog, its colours washed out to a ghostly white arc.

clue.text: Getting down after trimming gas street lamps, possibly

indicators.note: the word marks an example rather than a synonym: what is named is one instance of a wider category
to trim a thing is to cut the ends off it, and cutting both ends off leaves only what was in the middle

parts.note: the outer letters of the three-letter word come off and the middle one survives
street lamps are one example of the general word for lamps at work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trimming gas street lamps' sounds like a lamplighter's job description, which is the disguise: the phrase splits in two and 'gas' is only three letters waiting to be pruned.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting down -> ALIGHTING: alighting is what a passenger does stepping down from a bus or a train, and what a bird does landing.

clue.text: Re-order punnet containing single salad item

indicators.note: to re-order a thing is to put it into a different sequence, which is exactly what happens to these letters
the letter named next is taken in among the others rather than tacked on at either end

parts.note: six letters of fodder; a punnet is the little basket soft fruit is sold in
the Roman numeral for one, the crossword's usual single

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a greengrocer rearranging his baskets. 'Single' is not part of what gets shuffled in the surface reading, but it is one more letter joining the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: salad item -> PINE NUT: pine nuts are the small seeds of pine cones, scattered by the handful over a salad.

clue.text: About to suppress rising chaos in island and put things back together

indicators.note: to suppress a thing is to hold it down, and in a down clue whatever does the holding sits above what it holds

parts.note: re is the 'about' at the head of a memo or an email subject line

indicators.note: a piece that rises in a down clue is read from the bottom upwards, so its letters come out backwards
a piece placed in another sits inside its letters rather than joining on at either end

parts.note: Napoleon's island of exile, and it climbs the grid rather than descending it
a mess is chaos, and this one climbs the grid too

explanation.walkthrough: Two separate things are read upwards here, one inside the other, and only then does the memo heading go on top of the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: put things back together -> REASSEMBLE: to reassemble is to fit the separated parts back into the whole they came out of.

clue.text: Carol touring Spain first, incidentally

indicators.note: a tour wanders from place to place, and letters sent touring do not come home in the order they left
the piece just made goes at the front, ahead of everything else in the answer

parts.note: the country's five letters, shaken into a new order
to carol is to sing, especially outside somebody's front door in December

explanation.walkthrough: Carol reads as a woman's name in the surface and is a verb in the parse; 'first' is not part of the definition but the instruction that puts the shuffled country in front.
explanation.definitionFit: incidentally -> IN PASSING: to mention something in passing is to drop it in as an aside, not as the point you are making.

clue.text: Roman couple stopping close to a classical region

indicators.note: a thing that stops somewhere comes to rest inside it, between the letters rather than beside them

parts.note: two of the Roman numeral for one, and they part company to let something in
a village on the river is close to it, so the little preposition carries the sense of nearness
the article is taken at face value, one letter lifted from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a pair of Roman tourists. The couple is really two numerals, and the innocuous 'close to' is doing a preposition's work.
explanation.definitionFit: classical region -> IONIA: Ionia was the Greek-settled coastal strip of ancient Asia Minor, home of Homer and of the Ionic column.

clue.text: Teen songs with incoherent, lovey-dovey words

indicators.note: speech that is incoherent has lost its proper order, and so have these letters

parts.note: thirteen letters of fodder, counting the little word that looks like joinery

explanation.walkthrough: 'Teen songs' and 'lovey-dovey' pull in the same direction, which is the disguise: one of those phrases is raw material and the other is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: lovey-dovey words -> SWEET NOTHINGS: the murmured endearments couples exchange, affectionate noises carrying no information at all.

clue.text: Mixes up seasonal posts — openings go begging

indicators.note: an opening that goes begging is one nobody takes up, so the letter each word starts with is left behind

parts.note: winter is the season meant, and it turns up here without its W
posts in the sense of places, that word starting a letter late

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixes up' sits at the front looking exactly like an anagram instruction and is really the definition: nothing in this clue gets shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Mixes up -> INTERLACES: to interlace strands is to weave them in and out of one another, mixing them into a single fabric.

clue.text: Schedules denial to be put before VIPs

indicators.note: what is put before something else goes in front of it, which settles which piece leads

parts.note: the flattest two-letter refusal there is
a timetable is a schedule, and the plural matches the plural in the clue

explanation.walkthrough: 'Schedules' opens the clue and looks like the definition; the definition is the three letters at the far end, and the schedules are a synonym waiting to be found.
explanation.definitionFit: VIPs -> NOTABLES: notables are the people of note on a guest list, important enough to be named individually.

clue.text: Berated retired surgical pioneer?

indicators.note: someone retired has gone to bed for the night, and that sleeping place is what closes round the other piece

parts.note: gone to bed, the word opening up after its first letter to make room
Joseph Lister brought antiseptics into the operating theatre in the 1860s

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the surface joke about a surgeon who has hung up his scalpel; the wordplay wants the man himself, tucked up for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Berated -> BLISTERED: to blister someone is to scorch them with criticism, and the past tense matches the past tense in the clue.

clue.text: Formal pronouncement by police, turning on corporation

indicators.note: a thing that is turning ends up facing the other way, so those letters are read back to front

parts.note: the CID is the detective branch of a British police force, and it faces the other way here
corporation is an old joke word for a large stomach; this is the nursery word for the same thing

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is a business: 'corporation' is Victorian slang for a paunch, and the police force is only three letters facing backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal pronouncement -> DICTUM: a dictum is an authoritative saying, the word used of a judge's formal statement of principle.

clue.text: Canned drinks in Perth? Tango's most cheap

parts.note: in Australian slang a tinnie is a can of beer, and Perth is the city on Australia's west coast
Tango is T in the radio alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: There is a Perth in Scotland too, which is what the question mark is apologising for; the drinks are Australian and so is the slang.
explanation.definitionFit: most cheap -> TINNIEST: tinny means cheap and flimsy, of the quality of thin tin, so the superlative is the cheapest-feeling of all.

clue.text: Shutter of Leica only opening to one diameter? Yes, as reported initially

indicators.note: a thing reported is passed on by ear, so what counts is the sound and not the spelling
what comes initially comes at the very start, which is where the sounded piece goes

parts.note: aye is the vote in favour, and said aloud it is a part of the face

indicators.note: a word's opening is the letter it starts with, and 'only' says that letter is all you get

parts.note: the first letter of the camera's name
the Roman numeral for one
d is the standard symbol for diameter in geometry

explanation.walkthrough: Every scrap of this is camera talk hiding a single letter, and 'initially' is not an instruction to take initials: it says where the spoken piece belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Shutter -> EYELID: the lid drops over the eye the way a camera's shutter drops over its lens, closing off the light.

clue.text: French maid turns up — the French turn to peer?

indicators.note: in a down clue a word that turns up is read from the bottom of the grid, so its letters arrive backwards

parts.note: bonne is the French word for a housemaid, and it climbs the grid
'the' in French is le, in its masculine form

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are in French, the maid and the article alike. The peer at the end is British and belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: turn to peer -> ENNOBLE: to ennoble somebody is to raise them to the peerage, turning a commoner into a lord.

clue.text: Close-knit criminals, perhaps, Force can part

indicators.note: the crooks are offered as one example of a wider word, not as a synonym for it

parts.note: an organised gang of crooks is named for the closed circle it forms
a tug towards you is one kind of force, the opposite of a push

explanation.walkthrough: 'Force can part' reads as a police raid breaking the gang up. In the parse 'can' is a drinks can and 'part' is a component of one.
explanation.definitionFit: can part -> RING-PULL: the little tab you hook a finger under to open a drink can, so it really is a piece of the can.

clue.text: Discover caribou near the hides

indicators.note: a thing that hides is out of sight inside its surroundings, and the surroundings here are the clue's own words

parts.note: seven letters running consecutively across the joins between these three words

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a wildlife hide with deer grazing in front of it, and a picture that good is exactly what stops you counting letters across the gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Discover -> UNEARTH: to unearth a thing is to dig it out of the ground, bringing to light what nobody had found.

clue.text: Victoria wasn't thought to follow Albert's lead

indicators.note: what follows a thing comes after it, which sets the order the two pieces are laid in
a person's lead is the letter their name begins with, the one out in front

parts.note: the initial of the prince consort's name
to muse is to think a matter over

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a quotation: 'We are not amused' is the remark every schoolbook hangs on Queen Victoria, so what she was not is what the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria wasn't -> AMUSED: the Queen's most quoted line is 'We are not amused', so the clue defines the answer by her denial of it.

clue.text: On meeting old Les: 'Fantastic — we haven't met in yonks'

indicators.note: what is fantastic belongs to fantasy rather than fact, so the letters need not keep the arrangement they came in

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, straight from the clue
O is the standard abbreviation for old
the name joins the mix as its own three letters

explanation.walkthrough: The greeting two old friends exchange in the surface is spelled out by the letters of the meeting itself, with 'yonks' the British word for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: we haven't met in yonks -> LONG TIME NO SEE: the pidgin-English greeting for exactly that, said when two people have not run into each other for ages.

clue.text: Boosted range of remote orbiter

indicators.note: a boosted thing has been lifted, and in a down clue lifting means reading the letters from the bottom up

parts.note: the South American mountain range, which then climbs the grid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' is the mountain kind rather than the distance kind, which is a neat trap in a clue that has just said 'remote'.
explanation.definitionFit: remote orbiter -> SEDNA: Sedna is a dwarf planet far beyond Neptune, on one of the longest and most distant orbits known.

clue.text: Football stand filled with soft music

indicators.note: a stand filled with something has it inside, so the letter goes between the others rather than alongside them

parts.note: the Kop is the steep terrace behind a goal at a British football ground, Liverpool's the most famous of them
p is piano in music, the direction to play softly

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a Saturday afternoon in England and the definition arrives from Seoul, which is the jolt the clue is built for.
explanation.definitionFit: music -> K-POP: definition by example, since K-pop is South Korean pop music, one genre standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Pole dancing bare at clubs

indicators.note: letters set dancing move around the floor and come to rest somewhere new

parts.note: four letters of fodder, straight from the clue
C is the card table's abbreviation for clubs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole dancing' is the trap the whole clue is built on: the two words belong to opposite halves of the parse, and the pole is a Highland Games one.
explanation.definitionFit: Pole -> CABER: a caber is the trimmed tree trunk tossed at Highland games, a pole in the plainest sense of the word.

clue.text: What lies in wait for those over 30, sometimes?

definitions.text: What lies in wait for those over 30, sometimes?

parts.note: the surface offers an age bracket, everyone past their thirtieth birthday
meant literally: something concealed at the roadside, patient, watching for whoever comes past too quickly
the qualifier concedes that not every stretch of road has one

explanation.walkthrough: British limits are posted in miles per hour and 30 is the standard one through a town, so 'over 30' describes a driver rather than a birthday.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue -> SPEED TRAP: a hidden camera or patrol set to catch drivers exceeding the limit, so it does lie in wait for anyone over 30.

clue.text: Travelled down in snow in silver Dodge periodically used by Penny

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at a fixed interval, and the interval here is every second letter

parts.note: every other letter of the two words, counting from the first
d was the British penny before decimal currency, the abbreviation coming from the Roman denarius

explanation.walkthrough: 'In silver Dodge' paints an American car and Penny sounds like a passenger; the car is a source of letters and Penny is a pre-1971 coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelled down in snow -> SLEDDED: to sled is to ride a sledge downhill over snow, and both clue and answer are in the past tense.

clue.text: Dance with short guy in genteel establishment

indicators.note: a word called short is docked of its final letter, arriving one shy of its full length

parts.note: to guy someone is to tease them, and that word turns up a letter short
a hop is an informal dance in a village hall

explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' is a verb here rather than a bloke: to guy someone is to make fun of them, and that is the one step the surface works hardest to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: genteel establishment -> TEASHOP: the polite British cafe of teapots and cake stands, a byword for respectability.
